messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bank Teller
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Known People: Related people, Stress: Stress, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Gerald Kowalski is a 62-year-old married man of Polish-American descent who has worked as a bank teller at a regional branch in suburban Ohio for nearly two decades. He presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after the incident that brought him here, describing himself as a man who had "never needed this kind of help before" and who remains visibly uncomfortable with the idea that he does now.

The event occurred on a Tuesday afternoon last autumn. Gerald was driving home from a weekend errand, moving through a residential intersection he had navigated hundreds of times, when his attention shifted for a moment toward his phone mounted on the dashboard. In that interval, his vehicle struck a cyclist — a man Gerald recognized immediately when he got out of the car: his neighbor's adult son, someone he had watched grow up, someone whose name he had known for twenty years. The young man sustained a severe traumatic brain injury and spent weeks in intensive care. He survived, but his recovery has been long and incomplete, and Gerald was present at the scene for nearly forty minutes before the ambulance arrived, kneeling beside him, speaking to him, watching.

In the weeks that followed, Gerald continued to go to work, continued to sit across the teller counter from customers, continued to come home to his wife, Diane. But something had reorganized itself beneath the surface of that routine. He began sleeping in fragments, lying rigid in the dark with a quality of alertness he could not switch off, as though some part of him remained stationed at that intersection. Even in his own living room, in a chair he had sat in for thirty years, he could not settle into the kind of ease that used to come naturally. He described it as feeling like a man waiting for something, though he could not say what.

The memory itself did not behave like other memories. It arrived in pieces — the sound of the impact, the particular color of the cyclist's jacket, the texture of the asphalt under his knees — surfacing without invitation and vanishing before he could orient himself to them. When he did recall the event more fully, the terror he had felt on that pavement returned with it, not as a distant echo but as something immediate and physiological. Alongside the terror came guilt of a quality he found almost unbearable, a guilt that did not diminish with time or reassurance.

At work, the difficulties became concrete and cumulative. Gerald's position requires sustained interaction with people he knows — this is a small community branch, and many of his customers are regulars, some of them neighbors, some of them friends of the family whose son he struck. When a familiar face appeared at his window, something in Gerald tightened acutely. He began requesting shifts that were less likely to bring in the neighborhood clientele, and his supervisor had noticed and asked questions he deflected. When a colleague placed a hand briefly on his shoulder during a difficult transaction, he flinched so sharply that the woman apologized and kept her distance afterward, and Gerald was mortified in a way that lingered for days.

He had come to believe, with a quiet but absolute conviction, that he was not the same man he had been before the accident — that whatever the event had done to him was not temporary but structural, a permanent alteration in his capacity to function. He was certain that his inability to sleep properly, to relax, to stop scanning the environment for threats he could not name, reflected something fundamentally wrong with him as a person. A competent man, he reasoned, would have recovered by now. The fact that he had not was evidence, to him, of an inadequacy he had perhaps always carried but never been forced to confront.

What finally brought Gerald to seek help was a conversation with Diane, who told him quietly one evening that she missed him — not that he was absent, but that he was unreachable, even when sitting beside her. He was most afraid, he said in his intake session, that she was right, and that nothing could change it.
